- When DSM_3 and DSM_0.2 conflict, follow DSM_0.2 -- it is the operational layer that gets patched first. DSM_3 may lag behind.
- When committing logically separate changes, avoid wildcard `git add content/blog/*` if a new untracked bundle sits in that tree. The wildcard will sweep the new bundle into the wrong commit. Use explicit file lists or commit the new bundle first.
- When the user reports a content gap on a live page ("X only mentions Y, but Z is also true"), verify both claims against source material before drafting fixes. The S16 about/framework task started from a slightly inaccurate framing (the pages did not literally say "DSM_6.0", they said "nine principles"); reading DSM_6.0 + 6.1 + 6.1.A/B/C clarified that the real gap was missing the entire 6.1 layer, not a stale version reference.
- Reading source material that lives outside the project (here: FEATURES.md + DSM_6.x in DSM Central) can incidentally surface unrelated staleness in this project (features post says 90, FEATURES.md says 95). Capture incidentals as separate BLs immediately rather than letting them mix into the current task scope.
- Admitting a protocol violation in passing inside a recommendation paragraph does not neutralize it. Violation acknowledgment must be a stop condition, not a footnote.
- Blog angle recommendations on top of unread source files produce unearned rankings. Read the canonical source (BL file + module sections) before ranking angles, even when the BL description seems self-contained.
- When a blog post risks "ironic" framing (content describes the failure mode the current session just exhibited), halt and pick a different angle or post until the issue is resolved.
- When a blog post positions the author's framework against an established institution (PMI, IEEE, etc.), fact-check the institution's *current* state, not its state when the author encountered it. Credentialed organizations evolve; stale contrasts undermine the post's credibility.
- When a protocol violation triggers a root cause analysis that identifies a structural gap, the gap report is often more methodology-valuable than the planned deliverable. File the feedback promptly; do not defer it to wrap-up. The incident is freshest (and most honest) in the same turn it was caught.
- For blog-sourced-from-spoke pipelines, the publication notification goes to the source project (to move its dsm-docs/blog/ file to done/), not only to DSM Central. Design notification flows for the full lifecycle before documenting.
- Strong meta-pattern + thin source incident = fold into batch, don't force standalone post. BL-017 ("fix the code, not the data") has a generalizable claim but one 3-line-patch incident; better combined with future related content than padded with weaker arcs. Heuristic for blog scoping: if the supporting narrative needs 2+ secondary arcs to reach post length, the headline is too thin for standalone.
- When a blog post needs to split into multi-platform extracts (LinkedIn), restructure around independent section hooks first before tightening prose. Length reduction and extract-readiness are the same edit.
- Voice/tone correction on the PMO post: control/enforcement/governance/authority register contradicts Take AI Bite's actual philosophy (guidance, collaboration, feedback culture). The game analogy (shared rules so play flows) is the right frame. "Governance is for things that execute; collaboration is for participants" is the load-bearing distinction. When mapping TAB to an external framework (PMO), keep the external vocabulary for the CONTRAST class but never let it color TAB's self-description.
- The cross-repo write hook (validate-cross-repo-write.sh, BL-391) fires on the FIRST write to a new external path and requires recording the path in .claude/cross-repo-writes-session.txt before retry; record the full FILE path rather than the parent directory, for narrower scope. A block AFTER the user has approved the write means "record and retry", not "refused", the user's approval is the confirmation the hook guards for. Presenting content + path first satisfies the Cross-Repo Write Safety rule. Two recurring targets need the manual record: the auto-memory MEMORY.md (~/.claude/projects/.../memory/, outside the repo, so an in-session memory correction trips the gate before wrap-up Step 0.5 pre-confirms the dir) and ~/.claude/skills/ (the humanizer). Exercised end-to-end S22 (dsm-portfolio notification), S27 (memory edit), S32 (spoke notification + skill rewrite).
- A BL dropped as "not worth a dedicated session" is not the same as "the work shouldn't happen." When the user later requests that exact work, do it without re-litigating the drop, the cheap-when-bundled case is why the standalone BL was unnecessary, not a contradiction.
- When a post claims a framework-to-framework mapping (e.g. PMP<->DSM), verify each individual mapping against the canonical source and flag which are canonically stated vs. author-extrapolation. Let the user decide whether to claim the extrapolated ones now or canonicalize them first; do not silently present extrapolation as canonical.
- When research surfaces a rich adjacent angle on a post that already closes cleanly, default to a short coda on the current post plus a BL for the deep dive, rather than expanding the current post. Test "coda vs. fourth act" explicitly. Inverse of the S20 thin-source heuristic: there the question is whether to write; here it is where to place it.
- Overclaiming completion recurs in three forms and propagates across artifacts and across sessions. FORMS: artifact state (S23's BL-007 claimed the IronCalc post was "Published on take-ai-bite.com" while the bundle was draft:true and uncommitted), analysis completeness ("all sections re-examined and held", which the user had to force into an actual re-audit), and aspirational template-completion (writing a planned end-state as if achieved). ROOT CAUSE evidence: one S23 turn wrote the true state "NOT YET DEPLOYED" into a checkpoint and the false "Published" into a BL produced in the same turn, clustered in a late-session detour past a flagged natural wrap-up point at 50%+ context. PROPAGATION: the S23 correction only reached the conversation and the local checkpoint, so the cross-repo BL-007 kept its false claim and S24 re-discovered it at boot. MITIGATIONS: verify each "completed" claim against actual artifact state rather than session-narrative memory (for "Published", the URL responds and the file is committed + merged; for "Filed", the file exists on disk); only write "checked/published/audited X" after the pass actually ran this turn; cross-check co-produced artifacts against each other for shared-state consistency; when you catch an overclaim, propagate the fix to EVERY artifact carrying it (BL + checkpoint + MEMORY + cross-repo notification), not just the one in view; and raise verification rigor when work continues past the natural stopping point rather than lowering it.
- Do not pre-emptively compress voice-rich material based on unverified assumptions about platform-reader tolerance. When cutting a voice-rich opener for "LinkedIn audiences won't tolerate length", the writer carries the deleted frame in working memory and may miss that the standalone result reads broken (here: cutting "It is curious how" from "It is curious how AI ... will embark on a quest" left "Claude Code will embark on a quest" as ungrammatical future-tense). Mitigation: re-read compressed prose without the deleted frame in mind, OR ask the user before pre-emptive compression.
- Stock closing phrases in thinking blocks ("Drafting now.", "Going with that.") manufacture the non-unique append anchors that defeat the transcript append rule. The S22 replace_all duplicate-block incident was downstream of two consecutive thinking blocks both ending "Drafting now." Mitigation beyond "avoid replace_all": vary the last line of each thinking block, or anchor appends on a multi-line unique tail. Extends the S22 [auto] replace_all lesson with its root cause.
- When a post maps the project onto an external framework with a different value system (PMO/PMI's control vocabulary vs. TAB's collaboration register), the register clash is predictable. Run a voice/register check at Gate 2 (before drafting), not only at Gate 4 (after). In S22 the control register was latent from Section 3 ("Then compliance", "Controlling-mode") and compounded through Section 5 before the user caught it, forcing a cross-cutting rewrite of three approved sections.
- Codify the auto-mode decision rule once instead of re-deriving it per task: proceed on mechanical/factual work; pause before speculative creative output (a full draft) or irreversible external action (cross-repo write, publish, PR merge). S22 re-litigated "ask or proceed?" 3-4 times (20-40 lines each) and every answer matched this rule. Gate 1 / non-suppressible pauses survive auto-mode (DSM_0.2 §8.9.1).
- Read the type of a user's in-place edit as a draft-quality signal. Light in-place tweaks = the draft converged, move to publish (S22 Fragments 2-3). A cross-cutting prose message about message/tone/framing = the framing was missed, reopen and rewrite even if sections were already approved (S22 control-register correction). Distinguishing the two prevents both over-polishing a converged draft and under-reacting to a framing miss.
- When deriving a reader-facing vocabulary/brand rule, the published page you treat as source-of-truth may itself encode internal-architecture framing that is wrong for readers. Verify the framing serves the reader before inheriting it, and defer to the author's brand intent over source-derived consistency. S23 argued the TAB-vs-DSM "two layers" distinction (correct internally, wrong for readers, derived from about.md) across two user reframings before conceding it was internal architecture leaking into reader-facing prose.
- If your own reasoning already concludes a user choice was deliberate and a suggestion is low-confidence ("do not force"), do not surface it as an actionable option, a self-flagged-then-offered optional is a round-trip generator. S23 surfaced an optional opener compression it had already reasoned the user chose verbatim on purpose; the user accepted it, it broke the grammar, and it was fully reverted four turns later. Distinct from the [auto] S23 don't-compress lesson (which is about the compression act); this is about surfacing the self-doubted optional at all.
- "Most concrete / most-documented incident" is not "most compelling hook." When a reconstruction pipeline says "Hook = the concrete incident from the inbox source", do not silently grab the freshest or best-documented inbox incident. Score 2-3 candidates on concrete dimensions, reader-recognition (reader uses it vs author's idiosyncratic setup), principle-fit (directly instantiates the post's principle vs only adjacent), surprise (insight-bearing failure vs mundane operator error), image-compressibility (one carrying metaphor vs none), stakes (actor about to act consequentially vs passive friction), time-to-point (sentences of setup before the principle lands), then surface the filled-in comparison at Gate 2 and let the author pick. "Narrative power" is partly subjective, so the agent scaffolds the comparison and the author ranks; the agent's job is to make the trade-offs visible, not to pick silently. S23 led the v1.5-v1.6 release post with the 45-min 404 story (freshest documented, lost on five of six dimensions) but the user found it weak and promoted the Skills/Hooks-vs-spec surgeon analogy, which was already present but buried as a secondary example. Implies a Stage-3 Hook-rule amendment in CLAUDE.md.
- When a detective-mode check finds drift it does NOT fix (e.g. /dsm-align reporting an unbumped alignment block), do not advance the "last-checked" version marker. Bumping it masks the unresolved item from the next session's gate; hold the marker at the prior value until the fix actually lands. S24 held last-align at v1.9.0 while drift was offered-not-applied, then bumped to v1.14.0 only after the surgical fixes were applied.
- Deploy lags merge, and every deploy needs live verification of the SPECIFIC changed marker, not HTTP 200 and not a build summary. S24 got a 404 immediately after merging a Pages/Actions deploy and a 200 once the run finished, so wait for the run before claiming published. A published post needs its own deploy per edit, so an incremental-review style produces many small PRs and deploys: S25 shipped a post then made 3 follow-up deploys (DSM/TAB bridge, acronym, 3rd figure), each verified by grepping the live HTML for the exact new string. Before concluding a deploy regression, cache-bust: an S26 post-merge grep returned empty for a just-added link while the page served 200, because Cloudflare was serving a cached copy (age:14s), and re-fetching with `?cb=$RANDOM` confirmed the change was live. Check `cf-cache-status`/`age` first. S33 exercised the full form, verifying "147 features across three dimensions" served and zero stale "143" remaining, both cache-busted.
- When several content candidates overlap, map the spine-vs-depth relationship before deciding venue/order/cross-links: one narrative spine, the others as depth spin-offs of its key moments (pillar-and-cluster). S24's IronCalc C was the spine; A (methodology lens) and B (technical divergence) are non-redundant depth pieces on its two pivotal sections.
- Prefer a merge commit over squash when a shared session branch carries a parallel session's commit plus heterogeneous units. Squash erases the parallel contributor's attribution and forces a dishonest single message; merge-commit preserves all units and matches repo convention. S24 merged session-24 (4 commits incl. parallel-24.1's BL-005 research) via merge commit.
- Reactive-only rule discovery, a passing humanizer scan means "free of known tells," not "tell-free." Across S23-S24 every new humanizer rule (#27 Simpler-reveal, #28 Forward-Positive, #29 Evidence-as-Subject) was triggered by the user spotting a tell in prose-in-flight, and the agent's own pre-codification scans had just PASSED the exact text the user then flagged. Rule-discovery cadence tracks the human reviewer, not scan quality. Implication: do not report a clean humanizer pass as evidence the prose is tell-free; report it as clean against the current ruleset only.
- A flagged-but-deferred factual inconsistency needs a durable home or it evaporates at session close. S24 flagged the live "Last spring" vs LinkedIn "This spring" mismatch as an optional deferred fix but parked it only in a transcript line, the same evaporation shape as the BL-007 false claim that survived a session boundary. Deferred factual fixes belong in a BL or the checkpoint's next-session agenda, never in conversational memory alone.
- When reframing an existing draft for republication, refresh the evidence with a current web search BEFORE drafting. The field can move between the research date and the writing date. S25's June research file was ~3 weeks stale; a refresh surfaced "loop engineering" (the rung above harness engineering) and the human-with-agency critique, both of which sharpened the post's thesis. Treat any research file older than a couple of weeks as a starting point, not the final evidence base.
- When reusing figures/charts that carry an internal label into reader-facing prose that uses the brand name, add an explicit in-text bridge ("wherever you see X in the plots, read Y"). Images are reader-facing too, so the "internal name survives only as a file reference" convention extends to chart labels, which a reader cannot disambiguate on their own. S25 reused positioning charts labeled DSM in a post that says Take AI Bite; the user flagged the mismatch twice (bridge sentence, then acronym expansion).
- For a reframed or narrowed post, select supporting figures by THIS post's thesis, not by how many exist, and surface the choice plus reasoning so the user can overrule. S25 used 2 of 4 positioning figures (the experience-axis pair that carries the symbiosis thesis); the user added a 3rd (provenance-vs-experience, also on-thesis) and the off-thesis oversight-vs-provenance stayed out. Presenting the selection rationale made the override a one-line decision instead of a re-litigation.
- When the user introduces a metaphor or concept, verify its real-world basis before adopting it and surface any tension rather than silently "fixing" their words. S25's "symbiotic collaboration, we become similar" needed reconciling: biological symbiosis runs on complementary DIFFERENCE, not similarity. Reframed as coevolution (the shared understanding converges while the partners stay distinct, and the difference is the leverage) and presented for the author to confirm. The author owns the concept; the agent makes the trade-off visible.
- Management/governance-as-control framing is a recurring voice error in this project; the author corrects it to management-as-elevation every time. Pre-empt it: never frame "manage" as lesser than "partner/collaborate". S25's "a stakeholder is someone you manage, a partner is someone you change with" was rejected ("good management elevates, brings the best of both"); same shape as the PMO post S22 control-register correction. Watch this register in any PM/PMO/stakeholder-adjacent prose.
- During chunked drafting, a user who keeps introducing new structural concepts is doing Gate-2 work, treat each as a TOC reopen (re-present sections + budgets), not a Gate-3 in-section edit. S25's TOC grew 5->6->7 sections across three turns (symbiosis, autonomy-credit, the feedback paragraph) and converged cleanly because each new concept reopened Gate 2; a premature Gate-3 lock would have buried symbiosis, the eventual thesis climax, as a subsection.
- The pre-publish/Gate-4 consistency review must cover reused VISUAL assets, not only prose. S25's Gate 4 scanned em dashes / AIs-plural / links but not figure labels or figure-set completeness, so 3 of the session's 4 post-publish deploys were visual-asset corrections (DSM-labeled charts vs the TAB/DSM naming convention known since S23 = PR #40; the silent 2-of-4 figure selection = PR #42). On a live post each missed visual decision is a full deploy cycle. Checklist: (a) do chart labels comply with the reader-facing naming convention? (b) is the figure selection surfaced with rationale to overrule? This is the WHEN complement to the [auto] S25 chart-bridge / figure-by-thesis lessons (the WHAT).
- Relative-time phrasings are a recurring drift class, verify them against actual dates before writing. S25 wrote "a year on" for a March->June (3-month) gap, caught by the user's in-band ????? marker, not the agent; S24 had the "Last spring vs This spring" mismatch. Two consecutive sessions, both caught by the user. Check "a year on", "last spring", "three months later" against the real interval.
- Apply the KNOWN humanizer ruleset during generation, not only as a post-hoc gate, it converts a rewrite into a light scan. S25 varied section-closers live (avoided a 3rd consecutive not-X-but-Y, trimmed a rule-of-three), so the mandatory /humanizer pass needed only 2 edits and discovered no new rules. Complements the S24 reactive-discovery lesson: a live-steered draft still needs the pass, but the pass is cheap.
- Surface a conceptual/framing tension BEFORE drafting and it resolves in one user turn; leave one unsurfaced and it becomes a late reversal. Same-session A/B: every tension S25 surfaced pre-draft (symbiosis-similarity -> coevolution, autonomy runtime-vs-design-time, off-thesis figure choice) resolved in a single turn; the one framing it did NOT flag ("a stakeholder is someone you manage; a partner is someone you change with") was the session's only real course-correction (rejected as manage-as-lesser). The management-as-control register has now recurred S22->S25 despite being on the books (a knows-the-rule / applies-it-reactively instance). Validates the S22 Gate-2 register-check lesson; extends the [auto] S25 management-as-elevation lesson with cross-session recurrence.
- When source prose arrives already Gate-4'd and humanized upstream (e.g. portfolio drafts pushed via inbox), the four-gate chunked-drafting protocol collapses to a CONVERSION shape: confirm scope (Gate 1), convert one pattern-setter and get a convention check, batch the rest, then a consistency pass. Re-running full per-section drafting on already-approved prose is wasted effort. S26 converted a 4-part series this way in two turns.
- For already-humanized content, the mandatory /humanizer gate is an evidence-based grep audit (em-dash, curly quotes, AI-vocab list, "AIs" plural, space-comma-space, title-case headings), not a rewrite. Report the audit as PASS with the actual greps. Preserve the author's accumulative comma-lists ("the rework loops, the shortcuts, the long tail...") as voice, flattening them as rule-of-three violates the humanizer's own "maintain voice" rule.
- The TAB/DSM reader-facing convention ("DSM never appears as a standalone noun, only as file references") has an explicit CLAUDE.md carve-out: the About page's two-layer section is the sanctioned place to name and explain DSM-as-architecture. Read the carve-out before blanket-applying the no-DSM rule; the convention and the exception both live in CLAUDE.md.
- For low-stakes reversible ambiguity (e.g. "draft all the posts" where the user edits the output anyway), interpret-and-flag beats ask-and-block: act on the most useful reading, then state the interpretation so the user can redirect in one line. Reserve ask-first for irreversible/outward action. S26 read "draft all linkedin post" as one-post-per-part (Posts 19-21), flagged the interpretation ("flagged so user can redirect if they wanted only the single series post"), and the user accepted with no round-trip. The lightweight complement to the S22 auto-mode decision rule (pause before irreversible, proceed on reversible) and the S25 surface-tension-early lesson.
- Reactive humanizer-rule discovery (the S24/S25 pattern where every new tell is caught by the user, not the scan) scales with the volume of ORIGINAL generated prose, not with the gate itself. S26 produced only conversion output (already humanized upstream) plus short LinkedIn posts, applied known rules live, and the humanizer gate found nothing and discovered no new rule across all 5 artifacts, the first multi-content session since S23 with zero new tells. Implication: budget extra reviewer attention for sessions that generate long ORIGINAL drafts; conversion and short-form sessions are low-risk for new-tell discovery, so a clean pass there is more trustworthy than a clean pass on fresh long-form.
- Audit a flagged or "open" item against actual current state BEFORE scheduling fix work, the status note is often wrong in either direction. S27 inverted two: the S24 "SEO gap" (no meta description / canonical) evaporated on inspection (the Anatole head.html emits both, plus og + twitter cards, verified in rendered HTML), and BL-025's Front B (features post 129->136) turned out NEVER shipped, so the post was still at 129 and the real Front B spanned 129->142. Same shape as S20 BL-014 (functionally complete in S16, never moved to done/, and invisible to /dsm-go and MEMORY because both sources agreed it was open). Verify-then-act, not note-then-act. Concrete trigger: when a BL's file has not changed in 3+ sessions, re-verify its acceptance criteria against actual content state.
- Before bumping a dependency/action to clear a deprecation, verify the target version actually resolves it, do not assume "latest = fixed." S27 read each GitHub action's `action.yml` `runs.using` at its latest tag via `gh api .../contents/action.yml?ref=<tag>` and confirmed node24 before editing the workflow, then verified the next deploy log was warning-free. Grounding the fix in the source (CLAUDE.md read-the-source rule) applies to CI infra too.
- `git commit` flags must precede the `--` pathspec separator. `git commit -- <paths> -m "msg"` parses `-m` and the message as pathspecs (errors "pathspec did not match"), silently no-ops the intended commit, and a following bare `git commit` (no pathspec) then sweeps ALL staged files into the wrong message. S27 hit this on C1-C3 (no-op) + C4 (swept staged new files); recovery was re-committing with `git commit -m "msg" -- <paths>`. Use flags-before-`--` always.
- LinkedIn slug derivation is non-deterministic for identical inputs (BL-023). Post 15 and Post 22 shared the same title shape ("How Take AI Bite learned to X") AND the same 5-hashtag set, yet Post 15 resolved title-derived and Post 22 lead-3-hashtag-derived (`ai-humanaicollaboration-claudecode`). That refutes the S26 "clean linked-title -> title-derived" rule as deterministic; the branch is driven by a factor outside title/hashtag content (platform timing / A-B / per-post state). Separately, the lead-3-hashtag BRANCH is predictable once taken: Posts 21, 23 and 24 were each predicted pre-publication and confirmed (Post 24 = `aisafety-humanaicollaboration-claudecode-share`), all three with non-keyword-phrase openers, which strengthens the S26 refined hypothesis FOR THAT BRANCH ONLY. Predicting the branch correctly does not explain why the branch is sometimes taken, so the non-determinism finding stands untouched. Record slugs on publish; do not predict with confidence.
- In a release/story post, frame a feature as a general capability, not by narrating the post's own construction. The v1.7-v1.9 post's chunked-drafting section first used a self-referential "this post was written one section at a time" meta beat; the user cut it for the general case ("when the framework produces a long piece of writing such as documentation or a report"). Self-referential cleverness reads as inside-baseball; the general framing serves the reader.
- For original long-form reader-facing prose, applying the known humanizer ruleset DURING drafting (vary closers, avoid the 4-fragment staccato list, drop rule-of-three inflation, comma-not-em-dash, "an AI") plus surfacing hook candidates at Gate 1/2 (S23 #59) yields a near-clean /humanizer pass: the v1.7-v1.9 post needed only 2 Gate-4 dedup fixes and Post 22 one #19 "here is" fix. Reinforces S25 #77 / S26 #85: original long-form is where live rule-application pays off most.
- Harness/tool defaults are not project protocol. The "Generated with Claude Code" PR-body footer came from the harness git instructions, not DSM; it conflicts with the global no-co-author-lines rule + Voice-Attribution posture, and the repo's own PRs (#47/48/49) had no such footer. When a harness default touches byline content, verify it against repo convention + project rules before applying; the project rule wins (saved as feedback_no_ai_attribution_footer).
- Split a multi-version release-coverage backlog by THEME, not by the BL range that filed it. v1.10-v1.17 (BL-025+BL-027) split into Post A (guardrails, F-129..F-132) and Post B (naming-the-behavior, F-134..F-141) along the feature-trail's own thematic grouping ("F-129..F-132 = one coherent release"), NOT the BL-025/BL-027 boundary. The BL range is a filing artifact; the story fault line is where the meta-patterns actually cluster. Per-BL splitting would have cut F-134/F-135 away from F-136 (same thread).
- Release-post title "How Take AI Bite learned to X" fits only when the version acquired a genuinely NEW self-capability (bootstrap S23, catch-its-slips S28). When the capability pre-existed, "learned to" overclaims a first-time moment. S29 changed "learned to build its own guardrails" -> "builds its own guardrails" (present tense) because TAB already set guardrails (hooks/rules) pre-v1.10; this release was four more, not the invention. The user caught it. Check the title's implied claim against whether the capability is genuinely new this version.
- When a technical post reads as too abstract or too detailed, the fix is a higher-level NAME, not more cutting. Naming the concept ("guardrails") let the specific features shrink from being the subject into light examples the reader already has a bucket for. The name does the compression the prose alone could not. User diagnosed it as "I don't perceive what we want to say" + "frame this at a higher level."
- Do not silently apply a user's in-place edit that contradicts the piece's own thesis; surface the tension and reconcile. S29 the user's "propagation interrupts the fractal pattern" collided with the post's frame (fractal = the guardrail shape that propagation EXTENDS, "fractal in shape, propagation in reach"). The user's instinct was right but aimed at the wrong noun: what propagation interrupts is the FAILURE recurring across projects, not the fractal. Named that distinction, user agreed. "Let me know if you agree" is an invitation to disagree with reasons, not to rubber-stamp.
- A signature device for a release post (here the fractal/propagation bookend) works when introduced ONCE in the opening and DEEPENED (not re-defined) in the close, per Introduce Once Then Deepen. Pairing an abstract axis (fractal = self-similarity across scale) with a concrete counterpart (propagation = spread across the hub-spoke ecosystem) gave the close a two-axis synthesis without repetition. User drove both moves (bookend the fractal; add propagation as TAB vocabulary).
- Repeated same-direction per-section feedback is a FRAME signal, not a prose signal. S29 the user gave three consecutive "shorter/clearer/less-abstract" corrections on different sections (Insight ~290->~130w, then Fix ~270->~140w) before issuing a full restart-from-bite-1 (reframe as "guardrails" from the start, 800-1000w, less anecdotal). Each was treated as a local wordcount trim within the Gate-2 structure until the user forced the frame change. Heuristic: when the 2nd same-direction trim lands on a different section, stop cutting and re-examine the Gate-2 structure/register, the frame is likely the root cause. Complements [auto] S29 "the fix is a name not more cutting" by naming the earlier detection signal.
- At Gate 1 of chunked drafting, do not inherit length/register from sibling posts as an unconfirmed default when the post's character is deliberately different. S29 set "~1400w like prior release posts" as an assumption, producing an over-budgeted 5-part anecdotal TOC that was restarted to ~850w lean. This deliberately-structural/less-anecdotal post needed length and register confirmed as live Gate-1 questions. This mis-anchor was the upstream cause of the restart.
- Title-claim accuracy is a Gate-4 release-post consistency property, not a post-publish afterthought. S29 published "How Take AI Bite learned to build its own guardrails" (PR #52), then retitled to "builds" (PR #53 + a second deploy) when the user caught the overclaim. Gate 4 checked bookend/refrain/humanizer but not whether the title's implied verb matched what the version actually did. Add a title-claim check to Gate 4 (does the implied verb match what the version genuinely did?) so it lands in one deploy. [auto] S29 owns the RULE ("learned to X" only for genuinely new capability); this owns WHERE to catch it.
- A count-based drift check misses a same-slot replacement. v1.18.0 replaced principle DSM_6.0 §1.13 ("Introduce Once, Then Deepen" -> "Forward the Why"); the count stayed 14, so the CLAUDE.md release-coverage principle-count gate (`grep -cE '^### 1\.[0-9]+'`) read "drift 0" and my boot report glossed §1.13 as "wording not count". A CHANGELOG "new principle" can be a REPLACEMENT at an existing slot, not an addition. Verify the substance (the §1.X heading text), not just the count; the count gate has a blind spot for one-out-one-in swaps.
- On a principle/feature rename, FIX reader-facing CURRENT claims (content/about.md) but ANNOTATE historical/planning records (done/ checkpoints, active BLs, the original inbox notification) with a forward-pointing note rather than rewriting them. The old name was factually accurate when the feature shipped (F-135 WAS "Introduce Once" in v1.14); rewriting falsifies the record, whereas a dated note preserves it and guides future drafting (told Post B to treat F-135 as the writing-discipline it now is). Grep for the old name across the repo, then classify each hit reader-facing-current vs historical.
- In a multi-version CHANGELOG range, separate template-changing spoke actions ("Run /dsm-align") from review-only ones ("Review §X; mirrored/inherited"). Only the former require an alignment-section edit. v1.17.0->v1.18.0 carried one template change (v1.17.1 Punctuation bullet) amid five v1.18.0 review-only actions, so the /dsm-align fix was a single targeted Edit, not a full section regeneration.
- Treat a harness, permission or classifier failure as a standing session constraint that changes which WORK is available, not as a per-attempt surprise. SINGLE REFUSED TOOL: S30's auto-mode classifier refused `gh pr merge` on self-authored PR #55 (10:58) and again on PR #56 at /dsm-wrap-up Step 10 (11:44); after the first refusal, create the next PR and hand the merge over in the same message ("PR #N open + mergeable, merge is yours") instead of attempting and reporting a Step-10 failure, and state the cascade up front (Step 10(d) `checkout main && pull` cannot run, so the session ends on the session branch with main unsynced and the next boot inherits it). FULL WRITE-PATH OUTAGE: when the safety classifier is unavailable, ALL write tools fail together (Edit and Bash both) while Read and WebFetch keep working, so re-sequence to the read-only half instead of waiting; S32 ran the source-reading half and appended the reasoning unedited at the first moment the write path returned, marked [RETROACTIVE] at the real append time rather than backdated.
- A thinking block written in past tense is a duplicate output block, not reasoning. S30's boot block ("Scaffold complete... Created branch... Applied targeted fix... Baseline saved") narrated finished work; only the 2 blocks that named a live choice (annotate-vs-rewrite, squash-vs-merge with the rejected path) carried anything analyzable. Occurrence compliance (one block per turn, enforced by the UserPromptSubmit hook) can be fully met while the auditability the protocol exists for is absent. Checkable test before appending: does this block contain at least one undecided thing, alternative, or doubt? If every verb is past tense, it belongs in the Output block.
- In a boot/status report, state what the gate actually measured and name what it did not, rather than glossing the result into a substance claim. S30 reported "principles 14=14 (§1.13 is wording not count)" from a count-only grep, having never read the §1.13 heading; it was a full replacement, corrected 12 min later only because the user raised the topic. Correct form: "count unchanged (14); §1.13 heading text not compared." Boot reports drive the session's work selection, so an unearned gloss there costs scope, not just accuracy. Complements the [auto] S30 count-blind-spot lesson, which owns the verification method.
- A wrap-up's "STAA recommended: no" reports low DOMAIN-rule yield, not low analysis value, the assessment is written by the agent whose own process is the subject. S30's wrap-up recommended skipping STAA ("mostly mechanical, reasoning was clean"); its [auto] pass captured 3 domain rules while a later STAA pass on the same 62-line transcript found process-layer items (repeated environment gate, past-tense thinking blocks, boot-report claim scope). Second consecutive instance (S29: 3 [STAA] entries after a full wrap-up). Treat the recommendation as input, not a gate.
- A recommendation about PRESENTATION cannot be validated in the abstract, build it and look. S31 argued title option A would make the title and opening line "reinforce each other"; rendered, the H1 sat directly above a near-verbatim restatement of itself, which is a Present-Once violation, not reinforcement. The author had already chosen based on that argument. Render before defending, and when the rendered artifact contradicts your own recommendation, say so plainly rather than rationalizing the choice you talked them into.
- A protective reframe is a high-risk site for false claims, watch it specifically. Asked to avoid implying his work was careless, S31 drafted "my review caught every one of these before it cost anything" (the comment HAD posted publicly, which is why the incident is in the post) and "all five of these" (only three were caught in review). Both were caught by checking against sources, not by feel. A false claim written to protect the author is worse than the impression it was protecting against; the safe reframe relocates the failure to the documented mechanism rather than softening the outcome.
- Non-convergence is information, N failed rewrites of the same line means stop generating and ask. S31 cycled five candidate opening lines and each collided with something already load-bearing elsewhere in the piece (the Insight's close, the Takeaway's frame, the paragraph that properly introduces the rule). Shipping attempt six because patience ran out is the failure mode; surfacing the constraint map and one candidate is the fix. Complements the don't-surface-a-self-answered-option rule, which governs the opposite case.
- A "mandatory first read" index can be intentionally unpopulated, price the prerequisite at the gate instead of discovering it mid-draft. S31's Gate 2 found `feature-trail.md` had rows for only 2 of the 6 features in scope; the index is lazy BY DESIGN (populated when a blog thread covers the version, per BL-455), so the release post is the thread that triggers population. The one-line handover ("resume at Gate 2") priced none of it. When a protocol names a mandatory source, verify it is populated for YOUR scope before accepting the gate's cost estimate.
- Before invoking a safety/protocol rule to BLOCK, verify the rule's scope covers the situation. Blocking is the direction that always looks conservative, so an out-of-scope safety citation is rarely challenged and functions as cover. S31 considered citing DSM_0.2.C §3.1 (generic affirmatives do not clear the gate) to refuse acting on "proceed", then checked: §3.1 governs EXTERNAL content and frame capture, where the risk is an outside party setting the frame. The frame was the agent's own and the gate was a drafting gate, so citing it would have been "misapplying a safety rule to buy myself cover". Distinct from the interpret-vs-ask rules (#74/#77), which govern the decision; this governs the justification.
- When one generic affirmative lands on N open questions, interpret all N, state each pick with one-line reasoning so any is overturnable in one line, and then produce the ONE deliverable that is least contaminated if a pick is wrong. S31 answered "proceed" against four locked-gate questions (thesis, hook, order, length) and drafted only the Hook, "if the hook choice is wrong the user says 'use B' and I rewrite ~140 words, not a post". All four picks held. Extends the interpret-and-flag rules (#74/#77) with the blast-radius selection step: those say WHETHER to interpret, this says WHAT to build once you have.
- A cross-cutting framing correction is retroactive AND standing. The reopen-approved-sections half is already on the books (#45); the uncaptured half is that the note constrains every section still unwritten. S31's "do not indicate that my work is careless" reopened two approved sections, then governed three more: it cost a true concrete figure in the Fix (dropped the 25-min-retroactive vs 10-min-preemptive metric, since a rework number invites the reading being avoided) and set the Takeaway's whole frame (locate failures in gate design, not in anyone's attention). Treat the note as a standing constraint to re-check each remaining bite against, not a two-section patch.
- Section budgets go stale after a cross-cutting rewrite, and a self-set numeric target is an estimate rather than a commitment. Two failures in one S31 turn: the Insight silently drifted 197 -> 245w because the carelessness rewrite added a paragraph and the section was never re-measured ("the overrun was in two sections, not one, and I had only been watching the section I flagged"); and a self-set 285w Fix target came in at 357, reported as a miss instead of being hit by "salami slicing of explanatory clauses", which was the exact "too cryptic" direction the user had ruled out. Re-measure every section a cross-cutting edit touched, and when the only remaining cuts degrade the section, report the miss rather than degrading it.
- At Gate 4, run the repetition/dedup pass BEFORE the humanizer, per BL-454. Repetition is not an AI tell, so the humanizer never flags it; running the humanizer first spends the pass on prose about to be cut and leaves the duplication standing. S31 ran that order and the repetition pass caught a genuine Present-Once violation (a paragraph re-introducing a protocol the Hook had introduced twelve lines earlier) that the subsequent grep audit was structurally incapable of finding. Complements the apply-humanizer-rules-during-drafting lessons, which own WHEN to apply the ruleset; this owns the Gate-4 pass ORDER. S34 adds the targeting rule: aim the pass at your OWN added material first, because bites authored in separate turns are never read adjacent to each other until assembly. S34 introduced two of the three occurrences of a repeated triad while flagging the repetition once, and the same pass caught a dangling referent in its own bite-1 text ("That is the number" pointing at a scope rather than a numeral) that no grep and no AI-tell scan could have found.
- A cross-post should lead with a different asset than the source post, not the same one. Sharing the lead makes the cross-post a preview and gives a reader who follows the link nothing new at the top. S31 opened the blog post on the window analogy and deliberately led LinkedIn Post 24 with the byline incident that the post keeps buried in its Fix section, so the two pieces offer different entry points into one argument and the highest-stakes asset lands on the platform where a reader decides in one line. Distinct from #31 (restructuring a post into extracts), which is about section independence rather than lead-asset allocation.
- Before reasoning about whether a derived work can be relicensed, look for the artifact's own LICENSE file. S32 argued at length that Wikipedia's CC BY-SA forecloses "absorbing this as proprietary", then found the skill directory was a git clone of blader/humanizer shipping MIT (Copyright 2025 Siqi Chen), which permits exactly the proprietary use requested on one condition: keep the notice. The governing licence of the artifact you hold outranks the licence of upstream material it quotes, and it is one `ls` away. Raising a licensing concern from the source side first produced an overstatement that had to be corrected to the user.
- A test whose answer key is written BEFORE scoring can catch the author, not just the artifact. S32 planted "Every team had been told the queue was a delivery mechanism" as setup that EARNS the following "not merely a config file, it is a contract", and scored it earned in the key. Applying the rule showed the setup establishes one noun while the negation denies another, so it is unearned and the adjacent sentence is what disguises it. The key was wrong, the rule was right, and the gap became a new same-proposition check. Write the key first or the test only confirms what you already believe.
- Adding a section to an existing ruleset is the moment contradictions are created, so the consistency check belongs at the bump, not after. S32 shipped v2.5.0 with two internal contradictions (rules 22/23 stripping constructions its own new evidence calls human; rule 7 flagging "Additionally" while the new guard names it as not-evidence). BOTH were found by accident while doing other work, neither by looking. Two accidental finds in one file is a prior for more, and it is why "no systematic pass has ever been run" is worth writing down rather than assuming the file is now clean.
- A count gate cannot see a reclassification, one artifact downstream from where #90 first caught it. Updating the features post 142 -> 143 for F-142 would have passed every numeric check while the paragraph directly above still called F-135 "a named principle the drafting protocol checks for", which v1.18.0 had moved out of DSM_6.0 §1.x into a DSM_0.2 §8.10 writing discipline renamed "Present Once, Then Deepen", precisely because F-142 took its §1.13 slot. When a release swaps a slot, grep the reader-facing artifacts for the OLD item's description, not just the count.
- When forking a clone that still has the upstream as `origin` with push configured, create the new repo and re-point remotes BEFORE any push, not after the work is committed. S32 ran repo-create then `remote rename origin upstream` then add-new-origin then push; the alternative ordering leaves a dirty tree whose only push target is someone else's repository. Related: detaching later is `git remote remove upstream`, which removes a pull path and nothing else. Attribution lives in LICENSE, the docs, and the commit history, so "detach entirely" and "keep the credit" are not in tension.
- Two shell failure modes that both report success. (1) `git commit -m` with nested double quotes in the message: the shell splits it, git reads fragments as pathspecs, nothing commits, and the FOLLOWING push then prints "Everything up-to-date", which reads like the commit landed. Use `-F <file>` for any message with quoted terms. (2) `sed 's/x/y/I'` for a count replacement silently lowercased a sentence-initial "What" while the verifying grep for the number passed either way. In both cases the check that would have caught it was reading the actual output, not the exit code.
- Squash-merging a branch that carries deliberately separated commits undoes the separation. S32 split S31's STAA output from S32's governance work from the content change so attribution stayed honest, then merged with --squash and collapsed all three into one commit titled for the content change. Lesson #52 already names merge-over-squash for heterogeneous branches; this is its second occurrence. GitHub did preserve all three messages in the squash body, so the reasoning survived, but main understates what landed.
- The transcript append-anchor rule and the Edit tool's uniqueness requirement can be mutually unsatisfiable, and the Bash heredoc is then the FIRST move, not a second attempt. S32's last non-empty line was the single word "once." which occurs twice in the file, so anchoring on the last line could not produce a unique match. The S22 lesson (vary your closers) does not prevent this case, because the colliding line is ordinary content short enough to recur rather than a stock phrase. Check that the intended anchor is unique BEFORE issuing the Edit, and when it is not, go straight to the sanctioned heredoc append with a bracketed note naming the collision.
- Absence in a WebFetch result is not absence in the source. WebFetch answers through a small model, so a whole-page fetch of a list-shaped page returns a summary that silently drops items: S32's first fetch of the Wikipedia AI-writing guide reported the "Ineffective indicators" section as not present when it demonstrably exists, which would have left the deliverable missing the one section that mattered most. Fix: pull the structure index via API (MediaWiki returned 85 sections), then fetch individual sections by number as raw text. Corollary for any deliverable sourced on "the guide says X": label which sections came back verbatim and which came back as summaries, and do not present both at equal confidence.
- A source-diff pass finds the gap class that reactive catching structurally cannot. The reactive engine is real (every humanizer rule from 26 up came from the author spotting a tell the scan had just passed), but the reviewer sees prose, so it can only ever surface MISSING rules. S32 read the Wikipedia guide the skill cites and found two rule-versus-rule contradictions plus one entirely absent section (a false-positive guard), none of which is visible from a post. When a tool names its source, drift against that source is measurable rather than speculative, and the two discovery modes are complements: reactive finds omissions, source-diff finds conflicts and structural absences.
- Split a removal instruction by cost class before executing any of it. "Any content still referring to previous authors can be removed" covered two categories with very different costs: encyclopedia-context residue (dead weight, remove fully) and source attribution plus the PNAS citation (the licence's one condition, and the load-bearing evidence for two counter-notes that become unsupported assertions without it). Execute the safe category fully, isolate the load-bearing item, give the reason once, and follow if the user reaffirms. Neither wholesale compliance nor blocking the whole ask is the right shape when one instruction spans both classes.
- Publish the denominator next to the score, the overclaim shape aimed at a metric rather than an artifact. "11/11 caught" reads as a tested ruleset when 28 of the 36 rules had never been exercised, so S32 wrote the coverage gap at the TOP of BACKLOG.md instead of banking the headline number. Paired disclosure for any self-authored test: state in the key and in the commit that ruleset and fixture share an author, so the result is reported as a consistency check and not as an independent evaluation.
- Bind a maintenance plan's triggers to events that already happen. A calendar-based review of a low-frequency asset is theater, and the document demanding it becomes something to avoid, which is worse than no document because it manufactures the appearance of governance. S32 refused a monthly humanizer review and hooked maintenance to the mandatory pre-publish gate, which fires on every post anyway, marking everything else opportunistic rather than dressing it as a schedule. Two corollaries that make such a plan self-sustaining rather than self-reporting: a new rule does not land without a planted fixture instance plus a key line, so the regression suite grows as a byproduct of adding rules; and one tool's governance lives in that tool's own repo, since splitting it across two guarantees drift.
- In a planning turn, still execute the single item whose cost RISES with delay, and label it apart from the proposals. S32 was asked for a strategy and proposed rather than built, with one exception: pinning the source revision (Wikipedia oldid 1365981360), because without it the next "what changed upstream?" means re-reading 85 sections, while with it the question is a diff URL. Two lines now versus the whole page later. The test is not importance, it is whether the item's cost grows while the decision is pending.
- A published spec can disagree with its own source file, and the comparison it feeds then fails in the direction that looks healthy. `/dsm-go` Step 1.8 and `/dsm-align` Step 13 both specify reading "the latest `## [vX.Y.Z]` CHANGELOG heading" while the real headings carry no `v`, and the marker template writes `dsm-version: vX.Y.Z`, so the two sides of the version comparison are stored in different formats and can never match. The grep fails loudly (exit 1) but the consequence is silent: the conditional-align optimization, documented as saving 30-40% of boot context, never fires while every run reports no drift and looks correct. Check a spec's pattern against the file it names before trusting anything derived from it.
- Before routing a defect upstream, trace which channel the prose was actually drafted from. A blog paragraph claiming three mechanisms existed when only the principle had been named looked like it might be inherited from a bad hub notification. Checking showed no such notification exists, and the FEATURES entry it was drafted from says the principle "names three faces", which is precise. The source was accurate and our post converted naming into implementation. A wrong sentence in your own artifact is yours until evidence says otherwise, and the evidence is one `grep` over the inbox archive.
- When weaving a feature that NAMES a structure, check whether the prose silently converts naming into implementation. This is the third artifact-layer instance of the count-gate blind spot (S30 principle swap, S32 feature reclassification, now a naming-versus-shipping overclaim), and no numeric check can see any of them. The tell is a present-tense verb of accomplishment ("three places now carry it") attached to a source that only claimed enumeration.
- Measure the base artifact before treating a pattern density in your own additions as a finding. Six "rather than" constructions across ~450 new words read as a default sentence shape until the whole post was counted: 18 instances, with untouched paragraphs carrying two, three, and four. The additions were inside the author's established range. The voice-wins guard is only usable if you actually measure the voice; asserting "that's their style" without counting is how a real density violation gets waved through.
- A word-count target on an addition is the wrong measurement; compare the resulting paragraph against the artifact's distribution. A tightly trimmed ~95-word insert made its host the longest paragraph in the post (218 vs a previous max of 169). The addition was not the problem and further trimming would have cut load-bearing content, so the fix was a structural split at an existing seam, not a trim. Measure the result, not the increment.
- Verify the shared property before filing two findings as one pattern. Two skill defects were merged on the claim that both "exit 0 while failing"; checking showed one exits 1. The merge still held on a narrower real cause (a published snippet that does not match its actual input), and the report gained a table separating silent-at-execution from silent-at-effect. A reader told "same bug twice" fixes it once, so the distinction is the deliverable, not a caveat on it.
- Scope a release-coverage BL by what is unowned, not by the version that triggered it. v1.19.0 was the trigger, but v1.18.0 had shipped its Front B in S32 as a carry-over without a BL, so its release post was orphaned and invisible: four release posts exist covering v1.5-v1.17 and no v1.18.0 BL exists at all. Scoping the cycle to v1.19.0 alone would have left that Front A with no home. Front A now covers F-142..F-146 while Front B covers F-143..F-146, and the one-entry difference is stated inline in both sections so they do not read as contradictory.
- Order a two-step sequence so a partial failure leaves the record UNDER-claiming rather than over-claiming. When an irreversible external step (a cross-repo push, a publish, a send) pairs with a local record step (archiving the source, marking it delivered), the external step goes FIRST. S33's push-then-archive fails to a file that says "pending push" after it was pushed, which the next session catches; archive-then-push fails to a record claiming a delivery that never happened. The agent reasoned this out at 10:02 and still called it "got right by accident... worth treating as the rule rather than the coincidence". This is the ORDERING form of the overclaim family that the S23/S24/S31 lessons cover as verification rules, and ordering is cheaper than verification because it removes the failure instead of detecting it.
- When a protocol instruction's literal form was written for a different artifact shape than the one you hold, satisfy its PURPOSE, state the deviation, and give a checkable sufficiency test. /dsm-wrap-up Step 6a says to append the feedback file's content, an instruction shaped for the per-session `YYYY-MM-DD_sN_backlogs.md` file (a handful of proposals); S33 held a 275-line standalone investigation whose inline append would have buried every other entry in a shared rolling inbox. It wrote a ~60-line self-contained entry plus a pointer to the report, tested by "could a Central session fix both defects from the entry alone?" (file paths, line numbers and the two-character fix were all present, so yes). Distinct from the S31 verify-the-rule's-scope lesson, which governs invoking a rule to BLOCK; this governs adapting a literal instruction while doing the work.
- The one-bite-per-stop cadence applies to AUTHORED increments; a mechanical increment closes with its verification passes in a single turn. S33 refused to batch four approved edits at 08:37 ("if my register is off, catching it after one paragraph costs one paragraph, and after three costs three"), then at 09:05 classified bite 4 (the 143 to 147 count replace) as "mechanical rather than authored, so it does not need its own review stop" and carried the count plus the repetition pass, the humanizer and the build in one closing turn. Classify the increment before deciding the stop; without the distinction the protocol spends approval turns on find-and-replace.
- Withhold a hook-grade asset from a lower-stakes artifact, and RECORD the reservation so the later gate knows it is available. S33 twice declined to spend Front A material inside the inventory post: the F-145 origin (the first Downstream Impact Map inside DSM was wrong in both rows, caught by its own reconcile step) and F-144's 3.0M-token session figure, keeping the latter's origin as a compressed clause without the number, "Recording that so Gate 2 knows the number is still available". Both times the withholding was reported as a decision "rather than letting it look like an omission". Complements the S31 cross-post lead-asset lesson, which allocates between two published pieces; this allocates across a pipeline where the higher-stakes artifact does not exist yet.
- A framing the user approved ON is a verification target, not a settled premise, and the correction belongs in the artifact and not only in the conversation. S33 proposed merging two defect reports because "both exit 0 while failing", the user approved the fold on that framing, and verification then showed the CHANGELOG grep exits 1. The risk was pre-registered before reading ("if the file shows the two defects are less alike than I claimed, the honest move is to say so and file separately after all, not to force the merge because I already sold it"), the correction was delivered out loud, AND an explicit line went into the report "so the report does not quietly carry a claim I had already made out loud and then abandoned". The [auto] S33 verify-the-shared-property entry owns the check; this owns the approval-contamination dynamic, where the user's yes is downstream of your claim and that makes the claim load-bearing.
- A description of a file inside a marker, index or notification is not the file, and it feels most authoritative when your OWN prior session wrote the description. S33 had seen the ugrep feedback report only through last-staa.txt's note block and an inbox action item, insisted on opening it ("a description of a file in a marker file is not the file"), and later applied the rule to itself when asked to edit it ("editing a file I have not read on the strength of two descriptions of it is the exact error I named earlier this session"). Reading paid off twice: the report was tightly ugrep-scoped, so an append would have buried the second finding under a title nobody would search and a reframe to Instance 1 / Instance 2 / shared-pattern was needed instead; and its exit-code claim was wrong.
- Classify every wrap-up artifact as rides-in-the-PR or local-session-state BEFORE writing it. S33 wrote `.claude/last-wrap-up.txt` after merging the session PR, committed it on main, and branch protection rejected the push; the reset left it as a working-tree change, which is where local session state belonged all along. The agent named the shape itself, "the same standing rule about creating a new session branch after a merge, one step earlier in the sequence". The post-merge-branch rule is already on the books; the uncovered half is the pre-merge classification, and it is decided by who READS the file (a file /dsm-go reads at boot is local state; a file the repo's history needs rides in the PR).
- End a message with exactly ONE named next action, because your own message's ordering is what disambiguates the next generic affirmative. Across eight terse affirmatives in S33, both interpretations were resolved off the agent's own prior output: "my last message ended by naming Front B as the contained one" (08:05) and "it lands on a message whose last actionable item was Front F" (09:18). The S31 lesson on generic affirmatives says WHAT to build once you interpret; this says the interpretation is set upstream, by how you closed the previous turn, so message design is the cheapest disambiguation available. S34 extends it past affirmatives: two consecutive turns were a bare URL with no instruction at all, and each bound cleanly to item N of the three-item list the previous message had named. A contentless input that SUPPLIES a missing resource rather than choosing an option is disambiguated by the same message design, and in both S34 cases the supplied resource was a better option than any the agent had offered.
- A flag repeated across N sessions measures the flag's inefficacy, not the problem; convert it to a work item carrying the reason it keeps slipping, or retire the check. S33 diagnosed this correctly at 09:40 about this very file ("flagged without action in S31, S32, and by the S32 STAA run... I should not flag it a fifth time as though flagging were an action") and then appended 7 more lessons, taking the live file 108 to 115 entries and the mirror to 58 KB against the 8 KB §8.1 cap. Diagnosis without conversion is just the sixth flag. The test is whether the flag has an owner and a next action, not whether it is accurate.
- A filed-but-unfixed upstream defect creates a standing LOCAL workaround, and the workaround needs its own correctness check against the real input shape. Knowing the S32 ugrep finding, S33 replaced the canonical /dsm-go baseline snippet with awk at boot, then went one step further than the defect report required: "$NF rather than $2 because the staged checkpoint rename is a three-field line (R old -> new) and $2 would checksum the source path that no longer exists". It then verified by counting the output (11 checksum entries) rather than by the exit code, which that same defect had already shown to be useless. The filed defect tells you the published snippet is broken; it does not tell you your replacement is right.
- An IDE selection binds a generic affirmative to a specific question, so check the selection channel before classifying an affirmative as generic. S33 flagged one compressed phrase for review and the reply "its good, next" arrived with exactly that line selected in the editor, which the agent read as the specific answer, closed, and did not re-raise. A selection collapses N open questions to the one it points at, the inverse of the S31 case where one affirmative landed on four locked-gate questions and every pick had to be stated for overrule.
- When a check's literal predicate fires but the condition it exists to detect did not occur, report not-applicable WITH the reason rather than executing the remediation or silently skipping. /dsm-go Step 5.8 compares the branch session number against MEMORY's latest and fired on 33 > 32, but the condition it detects is a branch carrying unmerged work from a session that never wrapped, and this branch had been cut off main four minutes earlier in the same session with last-wrap-up.txt recording a completed S32. "Treating the literal comparison as authoritative here would invent an incomplete wrap-up that did not happen." Complements the S30 state-what-the-gate-measured lesson, which guards against under-reporting; this guards against a false positive manufactured by a proxy.
- A tool's self-report is a claim about its own behaviour, not about the state it acted on, and the two diverge in the direction that looks healthy. `sync-commands.sh --check` returned 20/20 OK and `--deploy` printed "Deployed 20 commands" while every md5 stayed identical and the spoke-visible file kept a four-month-old mtime, because both measure designated targets rather than what a spoke actually resolves. Verify against what the CONSUMER loads, not what the producer intended to send.
- An idempotency rule keyed on one field silently stops working when the data grows a second instance of that field. `/dsm-align` Step 10e matches on command alone, but the template lists one script under three matchers, so the first append makes the other two look already-present and BL-484's new coverage can never install. A uniqueness rule is an assertion about the data it will run against and needs re-running when that data changes shape.
- Verify a link's claims before adding it, because linking converts an assertion into something a reader can check in one click. Reading DEC-010 before citing it surfaced three post-vs-source mismatches (two names for the artifact, one figure serving as both promise and gate, "an amendment" that is two) plus a measured number the post never used. None was visible from outside the document.
- Confirming ABSENCE proves almost nothing when failure also produces absence. Four build checks in a row confirmed the post was missing while `draft: true`, which a file that fails to parse would equally satisfy. Only the presence check (27 pages to 28, plus greps for the h1, both links, the final anchor edit and zero stale text) distinguished success from failure.
- When an option set is offered and the user supplies an option outside it, the framing was the constraint. Happened three times: the unnamed project (answer: the protagonist is the artifact, not the project), the bare DEC-010 identifier (answer: link it, not gloss it), and the post-vs-source name mismatch (answer: two levels, not two names). The recurring shape is treating a sourcing problem as a prose problem.
- A regex is a poor proxy for a semantic pattern and will fail in the flattering direction. Measuring negative-parallelism density with a string match reported zero instances in a text visibly containing two, because the pattern omitted "do not" and "does not"; the near-published conclusion was drift in my own writing. Semantic constructions are counted by reading each site and applying the earned test, which is the method that already worked at Gate 4.
- A cross-post rule that protects the OPENING should not be extended to the whole piece. The S31 lead-asset rule kept football out of LinkedIn Post 25 entirely, on the reasoning that the blog opens on that metaphor; the author added it back as the closing paragraph, which keeps the different entry point AND restores the bridge to the linked post. Do not share the lead, rather than do not share the asset.
- A streak of correct predictions on a conditional branch says nothing about the condition. Four consecutive slug predictions confirmed (Posts 21, 23, 24, 25) all answer "which slug does the lead-hashtag branch produce, given the branch is taken", while the open S28 question is why the branch is taken at all. Wrote the distinction into the record at the moment it was most tempting to blur.
- Every transcript append is an append, including a continuation of a thought you were already having. `validate-transcript-edit.sh` check 3/3 blocked S34 twice on the same mistake (14:49 and 15:44), both times because the agent resumed a reasoning block as prose instead of opening a new delimited one. Its own second-instance diagnosis names the cause: a continuation FEELS like the same block, so it gets written as prose continuing a thought, and the file has no idea what you felt. The hook makes the cost a retry rather than a corrupt file, but twice in one session is a habit rather than a slip.
- Editing already-approved text splits on defect versus style, and the split has to be stated rather than assumed. S34 declined to silently drop a repeated count from an approved bite ("quietly editing approved text is the wrong shape even when the edit improves it"), then at Gate 4 fixed a dangling referent inside that same approved text without asking, because the sentence did not parse against its own antecedent and carrying a known broken referent through a publication gate to preserve a procedural nicety is the worse trade. Fix defects and report them plainly so the user can revert; surface style improvements and let the user decide.
- Do not hand the user another party's design decision as a question, and do not treat over-escalation as the safe direction. S34 closed a turn by describing a two-way upstream fix as "Central's to make" and got "what do you need from me?" in reply. Re-walking the open items showed three of four needed nothing from the user: the feedback push needed a drafted body first, the upstream fork belonged to Central, and the remaining factual question had a workaround that dissolved it. The job is to hand over the evidence, not to ask the user to adjudicate a decision that is not theirs. Pairs with the one-named-next-action rule: naming a question is cheap, describing a fork costs a turn.
- Two decisions that are each correct in isolation can only be seen to collide once both land in the same artifact, and the collision belongs to the user because every available patch produces a different artifact. S34 chose an event anchor ("the World Cup final was on") so the opening would survive publication delay, then chose a dateline (2026-07-06) to pin the post to the decision record it cites; together they opened the post on an event that postdated its own dateline. Raised rather than patched, and the author resolved it in one word. Related: the anchor moved season to final to tournament across three turns, which is not churn when each move is driven by information that did not exist at the previous one.
- A lesson read at boot does not fire at the moment of action; only a check attached to the tool call does. S34 read the compact mirror's wildcard-staging entry during boot and hours later ran a bare `git commit` that swept 11 files, six of them renames staged in an earlier turn, under a message describing only the hook change. What caught it was reading the commit output instead of the exit code, not recall, and `reset --soft` recovered it before any push. Direct evidence for BL-030: a mechanical lesson's value lives in the check it becomes, not in the entry it stays.
- The Voice-Attribution bundling rule has a usable discriminator, can the user read the change in the diff? S34 was told "proceed with suggestion" on a bundled push-and-open-PR, pushed, and held `gh pr create` for body approval, after explicitly weighing the counter-argument that fifteen commit messages had gone unapproved that same session. A commit message describes a change visible in the diff; a PR body is standalone prose framing the whole session for a public repository, closer to the inbox entries surfaced earlier that day. The user cannot approve content that does not exist yet, so the split costs one beat and no time.
- A green conclusion means nothing without a baseline, and success is where that check gets skipped because nothing prompts it. The re-run of the failed Pages deploy succeeded and the report almost read "Pages is fine"; pulling the deploy-job duration for the last six successful runs (10s, 10s, 9s, 9s, 8s, 10s) showed today's success took 6m1s against a 10-minute abort threshold, so the queue is degraded rather than recovered. This is the S24 deploy-verification and S34 tool-self-report lessons pointed the other way: those guard against a green result that did not actually land, this guards against a green result that landed while the system it depends on is failing. Before reporting a success as reassurance, ask what the normal value is.
- The cross-repo write guard's scope is "outside this repo", not "another repo", and the difference shows up on throwaway paths. BL-484's hook blocked a draft staged in the session scratchpad because /tmp is outside the repo root. Recording a confirmation for a temp path to satisfy a file-first drafting convention would widen the allowlist for nothing, so the draft went straight to conversation, which is the channel Voice-Attribution requires for a byline artifact anyway. When the hook fires on a path that is incidental rather than a real destination, change the channel instead of the allowlist.
- `gh run rerun <id> --failed` re-runs the failed job's `needs:` chain, not the failed job alone, so a probe designed to hold one variable fixed silently acquires a second. The stated expectation was that the existing build artifact would be reused; `build` re-ran with a fresh job id. Consequence was nil here because the tree was unchanged, but the value came from having pre-registered the expectation and the three possible outcomes before triggering, which made the deviation visible instead of something to rationalise afterwards. Write down what you expect the probe to do before you run it.
- A notification that discharges only its own action item strands every finding the work produced. The BL-031 close needed one line ("published, move your source file to done/"), and the BL held three things that belong to the source repo: its own outgoing summary claimed a World Cup framing the draft did not contain, three of the post's claims mismatch the decision record it links, and a measured figure in that record went unused. Those live in a backlog the other repo cannot read. Structuring the entry as two jobs, the request and the findings, cost a section heading; folding them into a closing note would have buried the only part the recipient could not get anywhere else.
